candidate.answerReason: The intersections satisfy EP/EF=4/7 and EQ/EF=6/13. Their difference is PQ/EF=10/91, agreeing with D.

methods.label: Locate the intersections using similar triangles
methods.explanation:
Because all the requested lengths lie on \(EF\), we can locate \(P\) and \(Q\) as fractions of that segment. The parallel sides of the rectangle provide similar triangles.

First,
\[
AE=5-1=4,\qquad CF=5-2=3.
\]
Since \(AE\parallel CF\) and the angles at \(P\) are vertical angles, \(\triangle AEP\sim\triangle CFP\) by two equal angles. Corresponding sides give
\[
\frac{EP}{PF}=\frac{AE}{CF}=\frac43.
\]
Thus \(EF\) consists of seven proportional parts, four of which form \(EP\), so \(EP/EF=4/7\).

To obtain a similar comparison for \(Q\), extend \(AG\) to meet line \(CD\) beyond \(C\) at \(H\). We have \(BG=4-1=3\). The right triangles \(ABG\) and \(HCG\) have equal vertical angles at \(G\), so they are similar. Therefore
\[
\frac{CH}{AB}=\frac{CG}{BG}=\frac13,
\qquad CH=\frac53.
\]
It follows that
\[
FH=FC+CH=3+\frac53=\frac{14}{3}.
\]
Now \(AE\parallel HF\), and the angles at \(Q\) are vertical angles. Hence \(\triangle AEQ\sim\triangle HFQ\), giving
\[
\frac{EQ}{QF}=\frac{AE}{HF}
=\frac{4}{14/3}=\frac67.
\]
Thus \(EQ/EF=6/13\). Since \(0<6/13<4/7<1\), the order along the segment is \(E,Q,P,F\). Consequently
\[
\frac{PQ}{EF}
=\frac{EP}{EF}-\frac{EQ}{EF}
=\frac47-\frac6{13}
=\boxed{\frac{10}{91}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses parallel-line angles, vertical angles, AA similarity, and numerical proportions, all within elementary AMC 10 geometry.

methods.label: Use line equations and horizontal separations
methods.explanation:
Coordinates turn the two intersections into simple linear equations. Place
\[
A=(0,0),\quad B=(5,0),\quad C=(5,4),\quad D=(0,4).
\]
The specified side lengths then give
\[
E=(4,0),\qquad F=(2,4),\qquad G=(5,3).
\]
The equations of the relevant lines, found from their endpoints, are
\[
EF:\ y=8-2x,\qquad
AC:\ y=\frac45x,\qquad
AG:\ y=\frac35x.
\]
At \(P\), the equations of \(EF\) and \(AC\) agree, so
\[
\frac45x=8-2x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_P=\frac{20}{7}.
\]
Likewise, at \(Q\),
\[
\frac35x=8-2x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_Q=\frac{40}{13}.
\]
Both horizontal coordinates lie between \(2\) and \(4\), so these intersections lie on \(EF\); they also lie on the specified segments from \(A\).

We can use horizontal separations to compare lengths along \(EF\). Its equation shows that a horizontal separation \(d>0\) corresponds to a vertical separation \(2d\). By the Pythagorean theorem, the corresponding segment length is
\[
\sqrt{d^2+(2d)^2}=\sqrt5\,d.
\]
This common factor cancels in the ratio. Since \(x_Q-x_P=20/91>0\),
\[
\frac{PQ}{EF}
=\frac{x_Q-x_P}{4-2}
=\frac{\frac{40}{13}-\frac{20}{7}}{2}
=\boxed{\frac{10}{91}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses school coordinate geometry, linear equations, substitution, and the Pythagorean theorem. The length conversion is derived directly without trigonometry.

candidate.annotationRationale: The route-neutral target is the ratio of two segments. Both methods use segment differences and numerical proportions. The first route establishes AA similarity and applies corresponding-side ratios. The second models the rectangle with coordinates, finds intersections through linear equations, and uses the Pythagorean theorem to justify comparing horizontal separations. These are alternative routes, not a combined set of requirements.
